title: Cicada Emergence Map: Which Brood, Which Year
description: Explore a state-level list of possible periodical cicada broods and a limited sample of GBIF observations.
summary_sentence: A brood listed for a state may occur only in part of that state; verify local ranges with current specialist sources.
quick_answer: The tool uses a built-in state-level brood list and cycle arithmetic; it cannot determine whether a brood occurs at the selected location. The map shows up to 300 returned GBIF records, not a comprehensive range or forecast.
steps_intro: Underground for 13 or 17 years, then a few loud weeks. Whose ground are you on?

body.t: A state-level list can be a starting point for research, but cannot tell whether an emergence will occur at a particular venue.
Check current local extension or entomology guidance for tree protection and confirmed local brood ranges.
GBIF observations and the state list can introduce the topic, but returned records are limited and not a complete survey.
Cycle arithmetic helps illustrate 13- and 17-year periods; actual local emergence patterns require specialist sources.
Thirteen- and seventeen-year cycles have a least common multiple of 221 years. Local co-occurrence depends on actual ranges and is not established by this tool.

body.t: A 17-year cycle after 2021 gives 2038. The state list alone cannot establish that a specific location belongs to that brood.

popular_table.title: Notable broods and their calendars
popular_table.intro: From published brood records (USDA Forest Service and university entomology) — last emergence plus period gives the next.
popular_table.note: The built-in list is a simplified state-level aid, not a mapped local boundary. Expected years are cycle arithmetic, not a guarantee of emergence.

faq: Soil temperature — nymphs emerge when soil at about 20 cm depth reaches roughly 18°C (64°F), usually after rain. The year is the brood's clockwork; the week is spring's.
Fifteen recognised broods in the eastern US: twelve on 17-year cycles and three on 13-year cycles, numbered I–XXX with gaps where broods have gone extinct or were never assigned.
No — locusts are grasshoppers. 'Seventeen-year locust' is a settler-era misnomer stuck to a true cicada (genus Magicicada), harmless to people and pets.

Egg-laying slits flag small branches ('flagging') and can set back young or stressed trees; established trees shrug it off. The underground years of root feeding are gentle. Netting protects saplings in emergence springs.
Those appear every summer in small numbers and are not broods — this map covers periodical Magicicada only; a lone August singer is a different insect entirely.
The tool does not identify county-level ranges. Consult a current specialist brood map for local detail.
